blocks.content: The ocean floor that gets pushed due to volcanic eruptions at the crest, sinks down at the oceanic trenches and gets consumed.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The seafloor spreading hypothesis was proposed by Harry Hess in 1961 to explain the origin of mid-oceanic ridges and continental drift.
Constant volcanic eruptions along the crest of mid-oceanic ridges rupture the oceanic crust, pushing new magma outward and spreading the seafloor.
Rocks equidistant on either side of the mid-oceanic ridge crest show striking similarities in age, chemical composition, and magnetic orientation.
Oceanic crust is significantly younger (under 200 million years old) compared to continental crust (up to 3,200 million years old).
As new oceanic crust is created at mid-oceanic ridges, older crust sinks into deep-sea trenches and gets consumed in the mantle.

rows: Continuously created at ridges and destroyed at trenches
Preserved over long periods; rarely subducted into mantle

items: Harry Hess formulated the 'Seafloor Spreading' hypothesis in 1961 based on Arthur Holmes' convection current theory.
The age of oceanic rocks nowhere exceeds 200 million years, whereas continental rocks can be up to 3,200 million years old.
Symmetrical magnetic reversal stripes parallel to mid-oceanic ridge crests provide crucial proof for seafloor spreading.
Mid-oceanic ridges represent constructive plate boundaries, while deep-sea trenches represent destructive (subduction) zones.
